directions.hypothesis: If the Black Queen mechanism (loss of genes for a leaked public good) is at work, each amino acid's free level should relate to its own pathway independently. If the pattern comes from a shared pool, free levels of different amino acids will rise together and the link to pathway completeness will vanish once total free amino acids are accounted for.
directions.outcomes: Support: the leucine and arginine link survives removal of the shared pool, and added leucine shifts the community toward fewer synthesis-capable members. Refutation: the link disappears once the shared pool is accounted for, or the amended community does not change.
directions.prior_work: PMID 37322284 and PMID 35592760 show how auxotrophs are supported in cultures, and PMID 31316056 predicts metabolites from sequences. None of them tests whether natural communities' synthesis completeness follows free amino acid levels once a shared pool is removed.
directions.question: Does the tendency for soil communities with less complete leucine and arginine synthesis pathways to sit in samples with more free leucine and arginine reflect cheaper uptake by auxotrophs (organisms that cannot make an amino acid)? Or does it only reflect a shared pool of amino acids released by cell breakdown?
directions.readiness_basis: Pathway completeness and metabolite intensities are already joined for the cohort, but pH, temperature and other abiotic covariates were empty and nearly all samples came from one study.
directions.test: Using the NMDC Multi-omics collection, take the 13 testable amino acid pathways, 11 of which showed the negative trend, with leucine and arginine strongest and almost all samples from one soil study. Compute, per sample, the total free amino acid pool. Test whether pathway completeness still tracks free leucine or arginine after removing the shared pool, and whether the other nine pathways with the negative trend follow the same pattern. Then run a soil microcosm experiment with leucine added versus not added, and follow the leucine-synthesis-capable fraction of the community by metagenomics over several weeks.
directions.title: Do communities short on amino-acid synthesis live where free amino acids are abundant?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show whether gene loss in natural communities is actually shaped by dependence on a leaked public good, or whether this is a misreading of sample-wide chemistry. This would change how community amino-acid exchange is modelled.

directions.hypothesis: The score difference between contamination and environmental isolates comes mainly from accessory metal-resistance clusters, and the difference grows with contamination intensity. Core metal clusters will not differ between the two groups when species are matched.
directions.outcomes: Support: the difference sits in accessory clusters and rises with contamination intensity, with core clusters similar in both groups, under both matching routes. Refutation: the difference appears equally in core clusters, or disappears when species are matched or when accession matching replaces name matching.
directions.prior_work: PMID 41601069 and PMID 33540257 link contamination to resistance at community level. PMID 37065130 reports Desulfovibrio fitness genes. None splits an isolate-level contamination signal into core versus accessory clusters.
directions.question: Within the dominant phylum Pseudomonadota, do isolates from heavy-metal-contaminated sites score higher on predicted metal tolerance because they carry more accessory (not present in most genomes of the species) metal-resistance gene clusters, rather than more of the shared core clusters?
directions.readiness_basis: The metal scores and isolation-source bridge already exist; the heavy-metal group is only 10 matched isolates, the score is a genome-based prediction, and the two name-based bridges disagree on coverage, so the size of the advantage is only roughly known.
directions.test: Using the Pangenome Collection linked to isolation sources in the Phenotype Collection, split each isolate's metal-resistance clusters into core and accessory for its species. Compare contamination versus environmental isolates within Pseudomonadota, separately for heavy-metal, waste or sludge, and industrial contamination, and for host-associated isolates, with species matched. Check whether the stepwise ordering by contamination category holds for accessory clusters only. Repeat using genome-accession matching instead of species-name matching, because the two bridges between the strain database and the pangenome give different coverage and suffix-stripping of species names may merge distinct clades. Compare against Fitness Browser metal-important genes in Desulfovibrio vulgaris Hildenborough, which showed no clear deficit in core share relative to baseline.
directions.title: Is the metal-tolerance advantage of contaminated-site bacteria carried by variable accessory gene clusters?
directions.why_it_matters: If correct, tolerance in polluted habitats tracks variable gene content rather than a fixed species-wide trait, which changes how contamination-site isolates should be screened and how tolerance scores are built. Accessory status alone does not show the genes were horizontally transferred; that would be a follow-up question.

directions.hypothesis: Genes predicted essential by the model but dispensable in the transposon data mostly have paralogs or alternative reactions absent from the model. Genes predicted dispensable but essential in transposon data are enriched for unannotated essential functions.
directions.outcomes: Support: backup routes are common in model-essential, transposon-dispensable genes, and the reverse set holds the unannotated essentials. Refutation: discordance is spread evenly across annotation status and redundancy, pointing to regulation or measurement.
directions.prior_work: PMID 18840283 used ADP1 knockouts to refine the model and report agreement after refinement. It did not ask which kind of hidden redundancy or missing annotation causes the remaining disagreements. PMID 36097170 shows that essentiality varies with pangenome content in another organism.
directions.question: For Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1 genes where growth-model essentiality and transposon essentiality disagree, are the disagreements mostly genes with alternative enzymes or pathways that the model lacks, rather than regulation or missing annotation?
directions.readiness_basis: Both calls and annotations exist for 866 genes, though only 15% of genes have model flux data and growth predictions depend heavily on added gapfilled reactions.
directions.test: Take the 866 ADP1 genes with both calls, of which 639 are concordant and the remaining 26% discordant. Split the discordant genes by direction. Using the Pangenome Collection and ModelSEED Biochemistry, count paralogs and look for alternative reactions that could substitute. Test whether either direction is enriched for unannotated genes, using the ADP1 pattern that essential genes more often carry pathway assignments than dispensable ones, and use the genes that change flux class between rich and minimal media (177 of 866) as a comparison group. Select the best candidates for double-deletion tests.
directions.title: Is disagreement between metabolic model and transposon data explained by hidden backup routes?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show which kind of model error dominates, and mark where essential but uncharacterized functions are most likely to be found.

directions.hypothesis: Freshwater biofilm communities rich in Burkholderiales and Comamonadaceae will consume some dark compounds, but no single isolate from the enrichment will grow on them alone. Consumption will need a pair or small group.
directions.outcomes: Support: communities consume dark compounds while single isolates fail, and specific pairs restore growth. Refutation: single isolates grow on the compounds, which would point to annotation gaps, or no community consumes them.
directions.prior_work: PMID 22026719 shows aromatic versatility is lineage-bound in Burkholderiales, and PMID 34612321 and PMID 40960580 note poorly understood terpenoid biology. None tests single-organism versus consortium use of compounds that lack known catabolic routes.
directions.question: Most compounds in the ENIGMA Carbon Census (74 of 83) have no isolate known to use them. Is that because their breakdown requires several organisms working in sequence, rather than missing annotation in single genomes?
directions.readiness_basis: The compounds and candidate sources are identified, but the isolates, enrichments and chemical measurements do not exist yet.
directions.test: Using NMDC Multi-omics and the Carbon Census compounds, choose the dark alkaloids and terpenoids with no pathway annotations. Inoculate freshwater biofilm (periphyton) samples onto minimal medium with each compound as sole carbon source, and confirm loss of the compound by chemical measurement. Isolate members, test each alone and in pairs, and sequence the enriched communities. Compare against the known-callable aromatic compounds as a positive control.
directions.title: Are dark carbon compounds consumed by consortia rather than by any single isolate?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that the unexplained part of environmental carbon turnover reflects community division of labour as well as unannotated enzymes. This would change how enrichments and isolate screens are designed.

directions.hypothesis: Prediction quality for amino acids and nucleosides falls sharply when only strains of the same genus are compared, because the model relies on gene sets that act as genus proxies. Metals, antibiotics and nitrogen sources depend on single accessory or regulatory differences that gene-content features miss.
directions.outcomes: Support: accuracy collapses within genus for amino acids and nucleosides, and the leading features are those that differ between genera. Refutation: within-genus accuracy stays comparable to the across-genus result and leading features vary within genera.
directions.prior_work: PMID 42271456 links genomes to optimal growth pH with machine learning and PMID 29769716 maps mutant phenotypes of unknown genes. Neither tests whether prediction survives restriction to strains within one genus.
directions.question: Binary growth on amino acids, nucleosides and tryptophan was predicted from gene content across genera, yet metals, antibiotics and nitrogen sources were not, and growth rate, lag and yield could not be predicted across genera. Does the prediction also hold among strains within one genus, or does it mostly sort genera?
directions.readiness_basis: The 46K strain-condition pairs are in hand, but continuous traits could not be predicted across genera and GC content was available for only 32 of 727 genomes.
directions.test: In the ENIGMA CORAL growth data joined to the Phenotype Collection and Pangenome Collection, compare leave-one-genus-out evaluation with within-genus splits for each condition class, restricted to genera with enough strains that both growers and non-growers occur. Measure what share of the predictive gene groups differ between genera versus vary among strains within a genus. For metal, antibiotic and nitrogen conditions, test whether accessory genes that vary within a genus separate growers from non-growers. Then choose strain pairs of one genus that the model calls differently and test their growth in the lab.
directions.title: Does gene-content growth prediction work mainly by recognizing which genus a strain belongs to?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show whether gene content truly predicts phenotype or mostly reflects phylogeny, setting the limit on predicting growth for new isolates within a well-sampled genus.

directions.hypothesis: Cells lacking lipid A and Fur survive only if cbb3-type respiration is kept low. Forcing high expression of the cbb3 operon in the rescued strain will kill it, while deleting cbb3 in a lipid A-deficient, Fur-deficient strain that has no sspB deletion will restore viability.
directions.outcomes: Support: forced operon expression kills the rescued strain and deletion restores viability in the strain without sspB deletion. Refutation: viability is unchanged by operon expression or deletion, so the buffering is a side effect.
directions.prior_work: PMID 35649364 shows that fur mutations and anionic sphingolipids make lipid A dispensable, and PMID 19520766 and PMID 30210482 define the Fur regulon and iron stress. None tests whether respiratory-operon buffering is required for survival.
directions.question: In Caulobacter, loss of Fur lets cells survive without lipid A, and a further sspB deletion dampens a group of respiratory genes (cbb3, cyd, fix-NOPQ) that Fur loss would otherwise raise. Is lowering that respiratory operon part of what makes lipid A loss tolerable?
directions.readiness_basis: Transcriptome and fitness data identify the buffered operon, but no strains altering its expression exist and transcriptomes were taken only in rich medium.
directions.test: In Caulobacter strains lacking lpxC and fur, with and without sspB, construct inducible expression of ccoNOPQ and a ccoNOPQ deletion. Measure viability, oxygen consumption and iron-related oxidative stress in rich medium. Use Fitness Browser Caulobacter data to see whether cbb3, cyd and fix genes carry fitness effects under envelope stress. Add iron-limitation experiments, since none exist in the compendium.
directions.title: Does silencing the cbb3 respiratory operon let Caulobacter survive without lipid A?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that rescue involves metabolic and oxidative-stress control as well as membrane lipids, since sphingolipid synthesis genes were not switched on. It would also redirect antibiotic-resistance models based on lipid A loss.

directions.hypothesis: Metabolic overlap with PA14 predicts inhibition of PA14 only modestly and predicts inhibition of ExoS-carrying cystic fibrosis isolates still less. Interference mechanisms, not nutrient overlap, will explain a larger share against those isolates.
directions.outcomes: Support: rankings differ between PA14 and ExoS-positive isolates, and strain-specific overlap does not predict inhibition. Refutation: rankings match and strain-specific overlap predicts inhibition about as well as for PA14.
directions.prior_work: PMID 27881418 shows environmental pseudomonads inhibit patient-derived Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and PMID 17873029 describes carbon preferences in sputum. Neither asks whether a nutrient-overlap rule built on one toxin-type strain transfers to the ExoS-dominant clinical population.
directions.question: All inhibition assays used PA14, which carries the ExoU toxin and makes only the Pel matrix, whereas among 291 cystic fibrosis isolates 94% carry ExoS and 5% carry ExoU, a very different mix from environmental isolates. Does a commensal's shared nutrient use with PA14 predict how strongly it inhibits typical ExoS-carrying cystic fibrosis isolates?
directions.readiness_basis: Genome-based classification of toxin type exists for 6,760 genomes, but all inhibition measurements were made with PA14 only and have not been validated against ExoS-positive or PAO1-type strains.
directions.test: Grow the 142-isolate commensal set against PA14, PAO1 and cystic fibrosis isolates that are ExoS-positive and ExoU-negative. Compare inhibition rankings. For each target strain, compute metabolic overlap using that strain's own substrate preferences, and test whether it predicts inhibition better than PA14 overlap. Use spent-medium and contact-free assays to separate nutrient depletion from secreted inhibitors.
directions.title: Do commensal strains inhibit cystic fibrosis-type Pseudomonas as well as the PA14 test strain?
directions.why_it_matters: A formulation designed on PA14 could fail on the strains patients actually carry. This would show whether nutrient competition is a transferable design rule.

directions.hypothesis: Most of the ecotype difference in the replication/recombination/repair category comes from transposase, integrase and recombinase genes, and the unknown-function genes that differ between ecotypes mostly lie next to those mobile elements. Core repair genes differ little between ecotypes.
directions.outcomes: Support: the category's ecotype difference largely disappears once mobile genes are removed, and unknown-function genes are enriched next to mobile genes, including within lineages. Refute: core repair genes carry the difference, or unknown-function genes are no closer to mobile elements than random accessory genes.
directions.prior_work: PMIDs 40644951 and 37154706 report enrichment of the replication/repair category in accessory or unique genes but do not ask whether mobile-element genes rather than repair genes drive it, and PMID 33423895 reviews how mobile elements shape pangenomes without testing this.
directions.question: In species that split into gene-content ecotypes, is the difference in the replication, recombination and repair category carried by mobile-element genes (transposases, integrases) rather than genuine DNA-repair genes? Is the unknown-function category's difference carried by genes that sit beside mobile elements?
directions.readiness_basis: Gene-cluster annotations and genome-level presence/absence for the ecotype species are in the Pangenome Collection; the work is a finer annotation split and a gene-neighbourhood check.
directions.test: In the 12 species with valid ecotypes, split every gene in the replication/recombination/repair category into mobile (transposase, integrase, recombinase, phage-type) and housekeeping repair (e.g. mismatch and excision repair), using annotations in the Pangenome Collection. Recompute the ecotype difference for each part. For the unknown-function category, measure how often differing genes lie within a few genes of a mobile-element gene, and compare with size-matched random accessory genes. Repeat the comparison within the major lineages of each species, since ancestry was not controlled in the original result.
directions.title: Are replication-and-repair ecotype differences really mobile-element turnover in disguise?
directions.why_it_matters: These two categories showed the largest ecotype differences, but the differences are modest (about 3 to 4 percentage points in category proportions), and shared ancestry was not controlled, so they cannot yet be called adaptive. If mobile genes carry them, they would be read as mobile-element turnover, possibly reflecting lineage substructure, not habitat-specific repair. That would also help reconcile adaptive-looking categories with curated adaptive markers sitting in the core genome.

directions.hypothesis: A small set of functional groups shows a clear environment association after removing evolutionary relatedness. Randomly chosen gene sets of the same size and frequency show none, so the near-zero whole-genome signal is a dilution effect, not an absence of habitat adaptation.
directions.outcomes: Support: some categories (e.g. transport, defense) exceed the matched random gene sets in many species, and the effect is stronger with isolation-source categories than with coordinates. Refute: every category falls within the random-set range under both descriptors, which would place the weakness in the biology.
directions.prior_work: PMIDs 29975997 and 33602135 report weak or nascent habitat association for single species, and PMID 23332119 argues habitat structures gene transfer; none compares functional categories against matched random gene sets across many species.
directions.question: Do particular functional groups of genes (transport, secondary metabolism, defense, mobile elements) track environment within bacterial species, even though whole-genome gene content mostly does not?
directions.readiness_basis: Gene-cluster presence/absence, annotations and isolation-source metadata exist, but the per-category, per-species distance correlations with matched random nulls need new computation.
directions.test: For the species in the ecotype correlation analysis, split accessory gene clusters by functional category. For each category and species, compute the association between environmental distance and gene-content distance while controlling for evolutionary distance. Build a null from random gene sets matched in size and prevalence. Repeat with organism-proximal isolation-source categories in place of collection coordinates, in free-living and host-associated species separately.
directions.title: Is environment's effect on gene content hidden in a few functions?
directions.why_it_matters: The corpus mostly finds that environment barely predicts gene content, including no difference between free-living and host-associated bacteria, the opposite of what papers on reef and fungal communities report. A functional-group signal would show the weak whole-genome result hides targeted adaptation. A flat result across all groups would point to the environmental descriptors instead.

directions.hypothesis: Resistance islands are less lineage-restricted than size-matched sets of independently occurring acquired resistance genes, because they move as a unit on mobile elements. Core, near-universal resistance genes are excluded from the comparison.
directions.outcomes: Support: islands show more independent gains and weaker clustering by lineage than matched acquired gene sets, and recur across species. Refute: islands are as lineage-restricted as, or more than, matched gene sets, which implies mostly clonal inheritance.
directions.prior_work: PMID 33602143 and PMID 20375036 follow resistance islands in single genera or species, and PMID 39233522 shows resistance genes tracking mobile elements in one E. coli lineage; none compares island lineage-restriction with matched acquired genes across hundreds of species.
directions.question: Within a species, are tightly co-occurring resistance gene islands concentrated in particular strain lineages, or scattered across lineages like horizontally transferred cassettes? Is that pattern different from single acquired resistance genes?
directions.readiness_basis: Island calls and genome-level resistance gene tables exist, but gain counting on within-species trees and matched null sets need new computation; the largest species (e.g. E. coli) were excluded by size.
directions.test: In the species with at most 500 genomes, take the detected islands and compare their distribution on the within-species genome-distance tree with that of random sets of non-core resistance genes matched on size and prevalence. Count how many separate times each island appears to have been gained along the tree. Check whether the same island appears in several species in the Pangenome Collection, and compare island-carrying species to those without islands.
directions.title: Do resistance islands spread as clonal passengers or hop between bacterial lineages?
directions.why_it_matters: More than half of species carry such islands, yet it is unknown whether they are inherited with the strain or repeatedly gained. The answer decides whether surveillance should track strain lineages or the islands themselves, and excluding near-universal core genes removes a partly artefactual contribution to earlier lineage-signal differences.

directions.hypothesis: Where nitrogen fixation and ACC deaminase occur, they are near-universal within a species, yet sister species in the same genus differ in carrying them at all. The lifestyle switch then happens between species, and the type III secretion system may follow the same pattern less clearly.
directions.outcomes: Support: within-species fixation is high, presence between sister species is patchy, and carrier neighbourhoods show more mobile signatures than the other markers. Refute: the markers vary within species, or sister species rarely differ, which would point to inheritance from a common ancestor.
directions.prior_work: PMID 29255260 and PMID 22792073 describe genomic features that distinguish plant-associated bacteria and diversity of plant-interaction traits in Pseudomonas, but neither asks whether the key genes are fixed within species and switched between sister species.
directions.question: After comparison within the same genus, nitrogen fixation and ACC deaminase stayed tied to plant association most clearly, with the type III secretion system a weaker case. For these markers, is presence fixed within a species but gained or lost between sister species?
directions.readiness_basis: Marker calls and species-level core status exist for plant-associated species; the rerun shuffle, sister-species comparison and neighbourhood analysis need new queries, and tree coverage is limited for many plant-associated species.
directions.test: For each marker, in genera with both plant-associated and non-plant species in the Pangenome Collection, compute the fraction of genomes carrying the marker within each species and whether it is classed as core. Count how often presence differs between sister species. Check whether carrier gene neighbourhoods contain mobile-element genes or breaks in gene order, compared with markers that did not stay tied to plant association. Because the original within-genus shuffle used only 200 repeats and no correction across 15 markers, rerun it with many more repeats and a correction, and treat the type III secretion result as provisional.
directions.title: Are nitrogen fixation and ACC deaminase fixed within species but switched between sister species?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show whether plant-association genes are stable within a species but move over evolutionary time between species, which bears on the higher mobile-element load of plant-associated genera. It would also say where to look for the mobile elements involved. The 64.6% core share measured for beneficial gene clusters as a group does not by itself show that these markers are core, so this must be tested marker by marker.

directions.hypothesis: If the weak methane-oxidation transcript signal is real, transcripts are higher in heated plots while pmoA and pmoB DNA abundance and methanotroph taxa are unchanged, so warming raises activity per cell instead of enriching methanotrophs.
directions.outcomes: Support: transcript ratios and measured methane oxidation rise in heated plots with flat DNA, in both horizons and across seasons. Refute: the transcript signal vanishes with replication, or DNA abundance rises as much as RNA, which would mean enrichment instead of activation.
directions.prior_work: PMID 38561130 saw higher methane uptake under warming without a rise in pmoA copies in a subtropical forest, and PMID 34512564 profiled warming-responsive transcripts at this site but reported carbohydrate and lipid enzymes; neither compares methane-oxidation transcripts with DNA or measures the process at this site.
directions.question: In long-term warmed Harvard Forest soil, do the higher transcripts of the methane-oxidation genes pmoA and pmoB reflect higher activity of existing methanotrophs rather than more of them?
directions.readiness_basis: Only a single sampling date exists, the signals are weak and confounded by incubation, so seasonal replication and process measurements are required.
directions.test: The existing data cannot settle this: the transcript signals were weak and did not hold up once thousands of gene functions were tested together (the pmoB mineral-soil signal was borderline even before that), only one sampling date exists, and horizon is confounded with incubation. Analysis: in the Harvard Forest warming data, compare pmoA/pmoB RNA-to-DNA ratios between control and heated plots, and check the NMDC Multi-omics warming or thaw studies for the same signal. Experiment: sample control and heated plots in each horizon across seasons with replicate cores, all handled the same way, measure methane oxidation rates, and quantify pmoA DNA and RNA by targeted PCR.
directions.title: Does long-term warming raise methane-oxidation activity in forest soil without adding methanotrophs?
directions.why_it_matters: Whether warmed forest soils take up more or less methane depends on this. If warming mainly changes expression, DNA-based community surveys would miss a change in a greenhouse-gas sink. The same experiment tests whether a warming-selected group of fast-responding taxa exists.

directions.hypothesis: Most metal-linked associations collapse onto a single shared multi-metal axis. Only metals with dedicated resistance machinery (mercury, arsenic) keep associations of their own after the shared axis is removed.
directions.outcomes: Support: most associations are explained by the shared axis, and the few surviving metal-specific hits line up with metal-specific fitness genes. Refute: many metals keep distinct association sets after residualising, matching metal-specific fitness genes, so specificity is real.
directions.prior_work: PMID 41539526 and PMID 30336790 relate metal gradients to community function across sites, and PMID 41848047 suggests co-selection by residual metals; none separates a shared multi-metal axis from metal-specific programs or checks them against fitness data.
directions.question: Chromium, copper, lead and zinc rise together in industrial soils. Do the many metal-linked gene-category associations reflect distinct metal-specific programs, or one shared stress response that every co-varying metal inherits?
directions.readiness_basis: The soil metal measurements and gene-category tables were analysed in a prior project, but whether per-sample metal values can be rejoined to genome-resolved data and Fitness Browser organisms for this design is not shown in the findings.
directions.test: In the soil metal dataset, extract the dominant shared axis of metal covariation, then retest every gene-category association with each metal's residual after that axis is removed, and with metals fitted jointly. Compare the surviving metal-specific hits with metal fitness genes in the Fitness Browser for organisms with copper, chromium, zinc and mercury experiments, asking whether metal-specific hits are enriched for genes with metal-specific fitness defects while shared-axis hits overlap generic stress genes.
directions.title: Do soil metals select metal-specific gene programs or one shared multi-metal stress program?
directions.why_it_matters: Reports of strong metal effects on community function, and the suggested energetic trade-off under copper stress, cannot be assigned to any single metal while metals co-vary. A shared program would mean metal-specific resistance gene panels overstate specificity, and would change how bioremediation and risk assessments use metal-linked markers.

directions.hypothesis: Most shallow-depth core clusters are confined to one genus or family and are enriched for mobile-element annotations. Ancient, widely shared proteins with no structural relatives are the minority.
directions.outcomes: Support: most shallow clusters occur in a single genus or family and are enriched for mobile-element annotation, in balanced clades too. Refutation: a large share spans many families or phyla, or breadth matches deep-family clusters once oversampled clades are removed.
directions.prior_work: PMID 21298028 shows horizontal transfer drives protein-family expansion, and PMID 38977308 traces the origins of species-specific orphan genes in the gut. Neither asks whether genes that are core within species yet have shallow alignment depth are young lineage-restricted genes, and PMID 41273079 reports structure coverage without breadth.
directions.question: Hundreds of thousands of core proteins have very few detectable relatives and are mostly unannotated. Are they young genes that became universal inside one lineage, or ancient proteins whose relatives are simply missing from databases?
directions.readiness_basis: The shallow-depth core clusters and cross-clade cluster membership exist in the lakehouse, but the breadth counts and the comparison have not been run.
directions.test: For the 415,603 core clusters with shallow alignment depth, use the Pangenome Collection and UniRef Clusters to count how many genera, families and phyla carry a matching cluster. Compare with deep-family core clusters. Compare the share carrying mobile-element annotation. Run it again with oversampled Pseudomonas and E. coli clades removed, to check that breadth is not a sampling effect.
directions.title: Are conserved proteins with few sequence relatives young lineage-restricted genes, not ancient ones?
directions.why_it_matters: If the proteins are young and lineage-restricted, the apparent conserved-yet-novel paradox is lineage-specific gene birth, and these proteins are not a hidden universal core. Structural-genomics groups should then target them for lineage-specific biology. If they are widespread and ancient, they are deep unexplored protein families.

directions.hypothesis: Truly dark genes with nutrient phenotypes sit next to annotated transporter or catabolic genes more often than later-annotated genes with similar phenotypes. Their phenotypes are limited to one related compound family.
directions.outcomes: Support: dark nutrient genes are more often next to uptake or catabolic genes and respond to fewer, related compounds. Refutation: their neighbourhoods and substrate breadth look like those of annotation-lag genes, or they respond to many unrelated nutrients.
directions.prior_work: PMID 29769716 and PMID 22125499 tie poorly annotated genes to conditions but do not compare truly dark genes with later-annotated genes for substrate specificity or genomic neighbours.
directions.question: Genes that stay hypothetical after reannotation are depleted in stress phenotypes and enriched in nutrient, mixed-community and iron conditions. Do they encode narrow-substrate uptake or catabolic parts that only show a phenotype on a specific compound?
directions.readiness_basis: Condition labels, dark-gene status and gene positions exist; the neighbourhood and substrate-breadth comparison is new.
directions.test: Take truly dark genes with strong nutrient phenotypes in the Fitness Browser and, from the Pangenome Collection, list their genomic neighbours. Compute the share adjacent to annotated transporters, regulators or catabolic enzymes, and the number of compound families each gene responds to. Compare with annotation-lag genes with strong nutrient phenotypes in the same organisms. Use organisms with the most conditions, such as Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 with 121.
directions.title: Do truly dark genes hold nutrient-acquisition roles that rarely tested substrates hide?
directions.why_it_matters: This would give a concrete functional class for genes that now look random. It would also explain the opposing stress findings: dark genes overall look stress-dominated, while stress is depleted among truly dark genes, and two stress comparisons (28.7% versus 43.2% and 43.3% versus 54.7%) remain unreconciled.

directions.hypothesis: Gains of phaC in discordant carriers are placed on branches whose environment was already highly variable. Closely related species without phaC are no more variable in habitat than those with it.
directions.outcomes: Support: recipient lineages come from high-variability habitats more than their phaC-lacking sisters do, in complete genomes too. Refutation: sisters match recipients in habitat, or the pattern disappears once metagenome-assembled genomes are excluded.
directions.prior_work: PMID 17113245, 24887088 and 33350471 infer horizontal transfer of phaC from tree incongruence within single groups. None asks whether recipients were already in variable habitats across the bacterial tree, and PMID 42203387 links the polymer to fluctuating environments without placing gains.
directions.question: Carbon-storage genes are common in plant, soil and wastewater species and rare in animal-associated ones, with the pattern in every genome-size class. In species carrying phaC outside its usual phyla, is the gene acquired after a move into variable habitats, or were those lineages already in such habitats?
directions.readiness_basis: Gene clusters and habitat labels exist; the gene-tree reconciliation and sister-lineage comparison are not built.
directions.test: Build phaC gene trees and species trees for the 311 phylogenetically discordant carriers and their relatives in the Pangenome Collection. Reconcile them to place gains. Compare the environment class of recipient lineages with that of sister lineages lacking phaC, using NMDC BioSamples habitat labels. Repeat on complete genomes only, because metagenome-assembled genomes have uneven gene detection and could mimic absences.
directions.title: Is phaC gained by lineages that already live in fluctuating environments?
directions.why_it_matters: This separates habitat as a cause of storage-gene acquisition from habitat as a correlate of ancestry. It would show whether feast-and-famine ecology selects for the polymer, or only keeps it.

directions.hypothesis: Pairs of dark orthologs share their strongest condition class more often than shuffled pairings do, but less often than annotated orthologs of equal breadth do. Agreement is lowest with the one Bacteroidetes, Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron.
directions.outcomes: Support: agreement beats the shuffled null but trails annotated orthologs, and is lowest in pairs with Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron. Refutation: agreement equals shuffled pairings, or does not fall with distance.
directions.prior_work: PMID 29769716 and PMID 22125499 infer functions from phenotypes in one or a few organisms. Neither checks whether widespread dark genes behave consistently across distant lineages.
directions.question: More than half of dark-gene ortholog groups are classed as kingdom-level, meaning the narrowest taxonomic rank containing all their member species is Bacteria. Yet 37 of 48 tested organisms are Pseudomonadota. Do orthologs of a dark gene respond to the same kind of condition in more distant organisms?
directions.readiness_basis: Ortholog groups, condition labels and fitness records exist for the tested organisms; the agreement scoring is new, and Bacteroides is the only non-Proteobacterial organism available.
directions.test: For dark ortholog groups with fitness data in two or more Fitness Browser organisms, score whether the strongest condition class agrees between organisms. Compare with shuffled gene pairings and with annotated orthologs of the same breadth. Split pairs into Proteobacteria-only and those involving Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron to see whether agreement falls with phylogenetic distance. Record how many member species and phyla each group actually spans, since kingdom-level only sets an upper rank.
directions.title: Does a dark gene keep the same phenotype in a distant, non-Proteobacterial relative?
directions.why_it_matters: It tests whether a phenotype found in one model organism can be carried to relatives that cannot be tested. If agreement is at chance, wide distribution alone would not imply shared function.

directions.hypothesis: The rise of resistance-gene count with environmental diversity is steeper than that of matched-size sets of other accessory gene classes, such as defense or metabolic genes, within the same phyla.
directions.outcomes: Support: resistance has a clearly steeper slope than random accessory sets in most phyla after openness is included. Refutation: its slope sits within the spread of random accessory sets, or disappears once openness is included.
directions.prior_work: PMID 38457973 and PMID 38039820 link environmental drivers to resistance diversity in specific habitats. Neither compares resistance against other accessory gene classes to ask whether the environmental scaling is specific.
directions.question: Species from more diverse environments carry more resistance genes with a smaller core share, and within most phyla open pangenomes carry more of them. Is this resistance-specific, or the general accessory-gene growth of generalists?
directions.readiness_basis: Resistance clusters, accessory status and environmental embeddings exist, but only 28% of genomes have embeddings and the null sets have not been built.
directions.test: In the Pangenome Collection, for species with several genomes and environmental embeddings, compute environmental diversity. Regress resistance-gene count and the counts of matched-size random accessory-gene sets on it, within each phylum. Compare slopes. Repeat with pangenome openness in the model, since openness correlates positively with resistance count in most phyla.
directions.title: Do species from varied environments gain resistance genes beyond other accessory genes?
directions.why_it_matters: If resistance is steeper, environmental exposure selects for resistance genes themselves. If it matches other accessory classes, resistance is a passenger of open pangenomes, which changes how reservoirs of resistance are predicted.

directions.hypothesis: Accessory genes cause strong growth changes mainly in the specific condition their annotation predicts (for example efflux genes under their metal). The core excess therefore reflects a mismatch between lab conditions and accessory gene function, not weaker accessory effects.
directions.outcomes: Support: accessory genes show a much larger growth change under matched conditions than under unmatched ones, which core genes do not, and the core excess disappears among matched-condition tests. Refute: accessory genes stay weaker than core genes even under matched conditions, so the gap is not a coverage artefact.
directions.prior_work: PMID 29769716 reports condition-specific phenotypes and PMID 38948139 shows fitness genes enriched in core genes in one rich medium; neither asks whether accessory phenotypes appear when the tested condition matches gene function.
directions.question: Genes with strong condition-specific effects are more often core than accessory. Is that because accessory genes were simply not tested under the conditions they serve, or because their effects are weaker?
directions.readiness_basis: Fitness data and pangenome core labels are in the lakehouse, but matching annotation-predicted conditions to experiments needs new curation and compute.
directions.test: In the Fitness Browser, tag each gene with the condition class its annotation predicts, such as metal transporters or efflux for metals and catabolic genes for the matching carbon source. Using pangenome core/accessory labels, compare how strongly mutants grow worse or better in annotation-matched conditions versus unmatched ones, separately for core and accessory genes. Restrict to organisms with many metal and carbon experiments, such as Desulfovibrio vulgaris Hildenborough, Pseudomonas stutzeri RCH2 and Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron. Then test a few predicted-condition accessory genes with targeted deletions.
directions.title: Do accessory genes show strong phenotypes only when the condition matches their function?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show whether 'condition-specific does not mean niche-specific' is a limit of lab panels or a real property of bacterial genomes. That changes how accessory genes are screened for function.

directions.hypothesis: The small set of accessory fitness modules is enriched for genes that sit close together in genomes and near mobile-element markers, which would explain their co-occurrence across strains. Core modules and cofit pairs outside modules lack this clustering. Failure of this prediction would mean the module signal reflects shared ancestry or prevalence.
directions.outcomes: Support: accessory module members cluster physically and near mobile markers more than prevalence-matched random sets, and the pattern holds in near-clonal strains. Refute: module members are scattered like random accessory genes, so the co-inheritance signal reflects ancestry or prevalence. If too few accessory modules are testable in any organism, the question stays open rather than refuted.
directions.prior_work: PMID 34499026 and PMID 32100706 show accessory genes co-occur beyond chance in pangenomes; this direction tests whether fitness-defined accessory modules are physically linked mobile units, which those papers did not examine.
directions.question: Gene modules defined by correlated fitness show a larger co-inheritance signal than gene pairs, with the highest values for accessory modules. That module result is fragile: the accessory-versus-core difference was only borderline, accessory modules were about 5% of the mapped set, and in one organism no module qualified. Do accessory modules, where they exist, travel together as physical units?
directions.readiness_basis: Module memberships, gene coordinates and pangenome presence/absence are in the lakehouse; the work is coordinate-based distance computation and matched nulls, limited by the small number of accessory modules.
directions.test: Take the accessory module families (fewer than half core genes) and prevalence-matched core modules across the Fitness Browser organisms. Take gene coordinates from the pangenome genomes and measure distance between module members and closeness to transposase, integrase and phage genes. Compare with prevalence-matched random accessory gene sets and with cofit pairs outside modules. Repeat within the closest-related genomes only, to check the result is not driven by ancestry. Report per organism, because the per-organism module counts do not sum to the headline totals and the accessory class is small.
directions.title: Could the weak co-inheritance of accessory fitness modules reflect physical co-transfer units?
directions.why_it_matters: It would separate real co-transfer from inherited relatedness for the one class of modules where co-inheritance looks strongest, and show whether fitness modules can be evolutionary units as well as regulatory ones.

directions.hypothesis: Iron-zinc cross-resistance is carried mainly by iron-sulfur cluster biogenesis and repair genes. Removing those genes weakens the iron-zinc correlation much more than the correlation of metal pairs that do not target iron-sulfur proteins, and non-metal stressors correlate with metals far less.
directions.outcomes: Support: removing iron-sulfur genes selectively lowers the iron-zinc correlation, non-metal stressors correlate much more weakly, and the deletions are sensitive to both metals. Refute: correlation is unchanged after removal and non-metal stressors correlate as strongly as metals, pointing to a general stress axis.
directions.prior_work: PMID 31586033 shows zinc excess raises iron demand in E. coli and PMID 37272830 links iron uptake to zinc, manganese and copper responses; they do not test a shared iron-sulfur mechanism across organisms or compare against non-metal stress.
directions.question: Gene-level fitness is positively correlated between nearly all metal pairs, and iron with zinc more strongly than expected, but that Fe-Zn estimate rests on only 6 organisms and no non-metal stress controls exist. Is this a general-stress signal or a specific metal-damage mechanism such as iron-sulfur cluster damage?
directions.readiness_basis: The correlation analysis uses Fitness Browser data, but the deciding deletion measurements under zinc and iron excess are new, and the Fe-Zn estimate currently covers only 6 organisms.
directions.test: In the Fitness Browser organisms that have both iron and zinc experiments (only 6 so far), recompute metal-metal correlations after removing iron-sulfur biogenesis genes, and compare with removing size-matched random gene sets. Add non-metal stress conditions (antibiotics, oxidative, osmotic) as controls in the same organisms. Then, in one tractable organism, measure deletions of iron-sulfur biogenesis genes under zinc and iron excess.
directions.title: Could iron-sulfur cluster damage underlie the cross-resistance between zinc and iron?
directions.why_it_matters: It would separate a specific chemical mechanism from a generic stress response in a result that currently reads as 'all metals are alike', and tell us which tolerance genes are worth engineering.

directions.hypothesis: In organisms where a universally essential family seems absent, orphan essential genes can functionally replace it: a member of that family from a relative will rescue depletion of the best-matching orphan, and these orphans share predicted structure or domains with the missing family more often than orphans elsewhere.
directions.outcomes: Support: genuine gaps remain after sensitive search, orphans in gap organisms show structural similarity to the missing family more often than controls, and heterologous family members rescue orphan depletion. Refute: gaps disappear under sensitive search, hit rates match controls, and rescue fails. Structure-search failure alone does not refute; only failed rescue does.
directions.prior_work: PMID 36097170 and PMID 42726091 define core and strain-specific essential genes within one species or family, and PMID 15035042 treats minimal gene sets; none asks whether lineage-restricted essentials substitute for a missing universal function.
directions.question: Some essential genes have no orthologs in other organisms and are mostly of unknown function, while a few families are essential everywhere. Do orphan essentials fill the roles of universal essential functions that appear to be absent in their lineage?
directions.readiness_basis: Essentiality calls and ortholog families exist in the lakehouse; sensitive homology and structure searches need compute and the rescue test needs new measurements.
directions.test: Across the 48 Fitness Browser organisms, list organisms where a universally essential family has no detected member although relatives have one. First rule out missed distant homologs with sensitive profile searches, since best-hit orthology misses paralogs, fusions and diverged homologs; apparent gaps that vanish are not displacement. For the remaining gaps, predict structures of orphan essentials and search for fold or domain similarity to the missing family, and compare hit rates with orphans from organisms with no gap. Then, for top candidates in a tractable host, deplete the orphan and test rescue by the relative's family member, which tests function without relying on structural resemblance.
directions.title: Do orphan essential genes substitute for universal functions missing in their lineage?
directions.why_it_matters: It would give a route to function for the largest class of unannotated essential genes, and show whether essential functions are conserved as roles while the genes themselves are swapped.

directions.hypothesis: PQQ-biosynthesis mutants are defective on quinate because the PQQ-dependent quinate dehydrogenase lacks its cofactor, so added PQQ rescues them but not the core aromatic pathway mutants. Iron-acquisition mutants are not rescued by PQQ; whether added iron rescues them is the open part of the question.
directions.outcomes: Support: PQQ restores quinate growth of PQQ mutants but not iron or core pathway mutants, and iron addition has a distinct effect on the iron mutants. Refute: PQQ gives no rescue of PQQ mutants, or rescues other classes too, indicating a nonspecific effect. If iron mutants stay unrescued by both, their cause remains unexplained.
directions.prior_work: PMID 3044290 shows quinate dehydrogenase is a quinoprotein and PMID 2855587 studies PQQ biosynthesis; they do not test genome-wide whether PQQ and iron gene defects on quinate come from separate cofactor demands.
directions.question: In ADP1, quinate-specific defects fall in aromatic degradation, Complex I, iron acquisition and PQQ biosynthesis genes. Quinate dehydrogenase is a PQQ-dependent quinoprotein, which could explain the PQQ genes, but the reason for the iron-acquisition defects is unknown. Are the two defects separate cofactor demands?
directions.readiness_basis: Deletion strains exist for ADP1, but rescue experiments are new measurements; the pangenome co-retention check uses data in the lakehouse.
directions.test: Grow ADP1 deletion mutants of PQQ biosynthesis, iron acquisition and core aromatic degradation genes on quinate, with and without added PQQ or iron, and on glucose or succinate as controls. Compare rescue by mutant class. Check in the pangenome whether species carrying the aromatic pathway also keep PQQ synthesis genes.
directions.title: Do PQQ and iron-acquisition defects on quinate reflect different cofactor demands of quinate growth?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show whether a 'support subsystem' signature in fitness data reflects a specific enzyme cofactor dependency, and whether the iron defect has its own cause, which explains part of why quinate behaves unlike other carbon sources.

directions.hypothesis: Resistance genes that are core are those whose products also serve non-antibiotic roles, such as envelope maintenance or stress handling. Within a mechanism class they should show fitness effects under non-antibiotic stresses and co-vary with non-resistance genes, whereas accessory ones should be functionally isolated.
directions.outcomes: Support: core resistance genes show more non-antibiotic phenotypes and stronger co-variation with envelope or regulatory genes than accessory ones of the same mechanism. Refute: the two groups look alike once mechanism is held fixed, which would point to mobility rather than physiological integration.
directions.prior_work: PMID 35873140 shows some efflux genes are core in one species and PMID 25861385 shows cost varies by drug class, but neither asks what non-antibiotic role could make a resistance gene permanent.
directions.question: Resistance mechanism strongly predicts whether a resistance gene is core or accessory, yet it does not predict knockout fitness cost. Intrinsic efflux pumps such as emhABC are more than 95% core, beta-lactamases are 54.9% core, regulatory genes are 6.5% core, and blaTEM, tet(C) and ant(2'')-Ia are 0% core. What besides cost explains this spread?
directions.readiness_basis: Resistance genes were already linked to fitness data and core status across 25 organisms, so the first step uses existing linked tables; the knockout step needs new measurements.
directions.test: The mechanism labels came from keyword matching on product descriptions, so first re-assign them from the gene annotations and check that the core-versus-accessory spread survives. Then, for resistance genes in Fitness Browser organisms with conservation status from the Pangenome Collection, compare core and accessory genes within each mechanism class. Measure (a) fitness under non-antibiotic stresses such as detergents, osmotic stress and metals, and (b) how closely each gene's fitness pattern tracks that of non-resistance genes across all experiments. Then knock out a core efflux operon such as emhABC in a host that carries it and test growth under envelope stress.
directions.title: Is a resistance gene's conservation set by how embedded it is in physiology?
directions.why_it_matters: It would separate resistance genes that are permanent parts of cell physiology from true add-ons. That changes which resistance genes can be targeted without side effects, and explains conservation without invoking cost.

directions.hypothesis: Resistance genes whose base and codon composition differs most from their host genome, an indirect hint of more recent acquisition, carry the highest cost, and cost shrinks as composition becomes host-like and prevalence within a species rises.
directions.outcomes: Support: cost falls steadily as composition becomes host-like, independent of singleton status. Refute: cost is flat across the composition gradient, or the singleton signal disappears when one gene-linking method is used for all classes.
directions.prior_work: PMID 25861385 and PMID 29439838 describe cost and compensation for resistance mutations, but they do not test whether the cost of native resistance genes decays with time since acquisition in genome-wide knockout data.
directions.question: Core and accessory resistance genes have identical baseline knockout fitness, yet a separate analysis finds that single-genome resistance genes are the costliest class. Is cost tied to how recently a gene arrived rather than to its core or accessory label?
directions.readiness_basis: Gene linking and fitness exist, but composition-deviation metrics must be computed from genome sequences.
directions.test: In Fitness Browser organisms with linked pangenomes, take each resistance gene's sequence from KBase Genomes and compute its deviation in base composition and codon usage from the host genome, together with within-species prevalence from the Pangenome Collection. Composition deviation is only a proxy and does not give acquisition history, so also check whether it separates singleton genes from widely shared ones. Ask whether baseline knockout fitness is predicted by the deviation among non-singleton genes as well as singletons. For a strain carrying a likely recent acquisition, run a competition assay between carrier and knockout strain without antibiotic.
directions.title: Do newly acquired resistance genes pay a cost that fades as they are integrated?
directions.why_it_matters: If true, cost is transient after acquisition, and the absent core-versus-accessory difference hides a time-dependent cost. That would help explain how resistance persists once acquired.

directions.hypothesis: Many of its costly dispensable genes are costly only in aerobic growth. They should lose their cost under anaerobic denitrifying conditions and be less rich in mobile-element annotations than the costly genes that stay costly.
directions.outcomes: Support: a large share of the costly set loses its cost anaerobically and is not mobile-element rich. Refute: cost persists across oxygen states and stays concentrated in transposase, phage and insertion-sequence genes, which favours genomic invasion.
directions.prior_work: PMID 32994326 shows gene dispensability depends on carbon environment in E. coli, and PMID 22448042 predicts loss of costly dispensable functions, but neither tests whether an outlier organism's costly set is an assay-mismatch effect.
directions.question: About a fifth of the genes in Pseudomonas stutzeri RCH2 (21.5%) are costly in the lab yet dispensable, far above the next organism (14.0%). Are they costly only because the lab differs from this denitrifier's natural anaerobic life, or do they reflect accumulation of costly mobile DNA?
directions.readiness_basis: The existing oxygen comparison in RCH2 is confounded with metal salt, so the decisive matched aerobic and anaerobic competition has to be newly measured.
directions.test: Existing aerobic and anaerobic experiments in RCH2 are confounded with the metal salt used, so they can only frame the question. Use the Fitness Browser to list RCH2's costly dispensable genes and compare mobile-element keyword enrichment and singleton share against the other costly genes. The decisive step is new: run pooled mutant competition in a defined medium under aerobic and anaerobic nitrate-reducing growth with no metal added, and see which genes change cost.
directions.title: Is one denitrifier's costly dispensable gene set a lab mismatch or mobile-DNA load?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show whether outlier organisms in cost surveys reveal real genomic parasitism or only a mismatch between assay and native lifestyle, which affects how lab-cost results are read as evidence for selection in nature.

directions.hypothesis: Metabolic ecotypes predict isolation environment better than core-genome subclade membership alone does, and pathways that vary within a species are those tied to nutrient sources of different habitats.
directions.outcomes: Support: ecotype labels carry environment information beyond what subclade labels carry, concentrated in nutrient-use pathways. Refute: environment is explained by subclade, or ecotype and environment are unrelated across species.
directions.prior_work: PMID 24465487 links metabolic flexibility to spatial distribution of communities and PMID 22928415 maps soil niche space by traits, but neither tests ecotypes inside species against isolation environment with phylogeny held fixed.
directions.question: Species with many genomes split into a handful of metabolic ecotypes by their pathway profiles. Do these ecotypes correspond to distinct isolation environments, or do they simply mirror subclades?
directions.readiness_basis: Pathway profiles and isolation metadata exist, but subclade structure and metadata harmonisation must be computed, and only a minority of genomes carry environmental embeddings.
directions.test: For the species with at least 50 genomes and variable pathways, cluster genomes by pathway profile in the Pangenome Collection. Score isolation-source categories using genome metadata, supplemented by NMDC BioSamples where strains link. Compare how well ecotype labels and core-genome subclade labels each predict isolation category within species, and whether the discriminating pathways are carbon or nitrogen utilization routes.
directions.title: Do the metabolic ecotypes within a bacterial species track where its strains live?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that within-species metabolic variation is ecological adaptation rather than neutral drift, and give a way to infer habitat from genome content. The planned niche-breadth test for these ecotypes was never run.

directions.hypothesis: Metal-important genes involved in uptake, cofactor biosynthesis or metal-dependent enzymes are strongly core, while detoxification and efflux genes for metals with no biological role are much less core, so the pooled enrichment is a mixture of the two.
directions.outcomes: Support: uptake and cofactor genes are clearly more core than detoxification genes, and the difference between metal classes shrinks after the split. Refute: both gene types are similarly core, or toxic-only metals are as core-enriched as essential metals.
directions.prior_work: PMID 34765088 reports that most cadmium-responsive genes in one Enterococcus faecium strain are core, and PMID 34432491 and PMID 40302248 map metal-tolerance genes, but none separates essential-metal handling from toxicity defense when asking about conservation.
directions.question: Removing genes also important under salt stress left core-genome enrichment of metal-important genes intact, and strengthened it for essential metals; cadmium and iron, each in one organism, moved the other way. Do essential-metal use and acquisition genes carry the enrichment, while toxic-metal defense genes are as variable as other accessory genes?
directions.readiness_basis: Fitness data and core status already exist, but gene function labels must be assigned and the cadmium and iron results rest on one organism each.
directions.test: In Fitness Browser organisms with metal experiments, label each metal-important gene by annotation as uptake or cofactor use versus detoxification or efflux. Compare core fractions from the Pangenome Collection for each label, for essential metals (molybdenum, tungsten, selenium, nickel) versus toxic-only metals (mercury, cadmium, uranium), after removing genes also important under salt stress. Repeat with organisms contributing more than one metal to see whether the split holds within a genome.
directions.title: Does essential-metal cofactor handling, not toxicity defense, drive core enrichment of metal-fitness genes?
directions.why_it_matters: It would explain why different analyses disagree about whether metal genes are core or accessory, and show that conservation of metal fitness genes reflects ordinary physiology rather than adaptation to contaminated sites.

directions.hypothesis: Within genera that contain both soil/sediment and non-soil genomes, soil-derived genomes carry xoxF more often than their non-soil relatives, and inferred gain events fall more often on soil branches.
directions.outcomes: Support: a consistent soil excess within genera across several phyla, with gains concentrated on soil branches. Refutation: the excess disappears within genera, or appears in only one or two lineages, which points to lineage composition.
directions.prior_work: PMID 38369453 found xoxF gene clusters in Acidobacteria and other phyla from weathered granite and soil but did not test habitat against lineage; this asks whether habitat is associated with xoxF within lineages.
directions.question: Does the soil and sediment excess of xoxF persist when only close relatives are compared, so that it cannot be explained by which lineages happen to live in soil?
directions.readiness_basis: Genome and habitat data are in the lakehouse, but the within-genus tree building and gain/loss reconstruction need new computation.
directions.test: In the Pangenome Collection, take genera with genomes from both soil/sediment and other habitats, using habitat labels from NMDC BioSamples where available. Compare xoxF carriage between habitats within each genus. Build genus trees and reconstruct gain and loss to see whether gains map to soil branches. Repeat in several xoxF-carrying phyla, including Acidobacteriota, where the enrichment already survived a within-phylum comparison. Use annotations from both sources, since they disagree for xoxF. This is observational and can show association only. Selection would need a follow-up, such as lanthanide-limited growth of soil and non-soil relatives.
directions.title: Is soil habitat associated with xoxF gain inside single lineages, beyond lineage makeup?
directions.why_it_matters: A within-genus association would show that the soil signal is not only a by-product of methylotroph-rich lineages living in soil, and would justify testing selection directly. It would also show whether xoxF can serve as a habitat marker.

directions.hypothesis: Lanmodulin-positive genomes with xoxF confirmed absent carry other lanthanide-linked functions (for example other PQQ alcohol dehydrogenases) or come from lanthanide-rich habitats, so lanmodulin is retained for lanthanide handling independent of methanol oxidation.
directions.outcomes: Support: confirmed xoxF-free genomes consistently carry another lanthanide-linked enzyme or come from lanthanide-rich sources, and the deletion changes lanthanide-dependent growth or uptake. Refutation: xoxF is found in nearly all of them once better searches are used, or they carry no other partner, so lanmodulin simply tracks xoxF.
directions.prior_work: PMID 30351021 and 35814700 characterise lanmodulin in Methylobacterium and tie it to the lanthanide methanol dehydrogenase; PMID 41023737 surveys the lanthanome in methane oxidisers. None asks what lanmodulin does where xoxF is truly missing.
directions.question: Among lanmodulin-carrying genomes, those lacking an xoxF call may truly lack it or may reflect incomplete annotation. If sequence-level checks confirm xoxF is absent, do these genomes use lanthanides in other enzymes, or for storage or detoxification?
directions.readiness_basis: The genomic screen is feasible now, but the function test needs growth and metal-uptake work in a lanmodulin-positive, xoxF-free strain.
directions.test: Take the lanmodulin-positive genomes in Beijerinckiaceae, Acetobacteraceae and Hyphomicrobiaceae and flag those without an xoxF call from either annotation source. Confirm absence with a sequence-profile search for XoxF clades and an assembly completeness check, and keep only confirmed-absent genomes. Search that group in UniProt Annotations and UniRef Clusters for other PQQ-dependent dehydrogenases and for genes neighbouring lanmodulin, and compare isolation sources. Then, in one confirmed xoxF-free strain, grow with and without lanthanum and delete lanmodulin to see whether growth or metal uptake changes.
directions.title: What do lanmodulin-carrying bacteria without a confirmed xoxF use lanthanides for?
directions.why_it_matters: It would separate lanthanide handling from methanol oxidation and show a wider role for lanthanides in bacteria than the methylotroph picture suggests. If xoxF turns out to be present, lanmodulin simply tracks it.

directions.hypothesis: The lanmodulin gene tree disagrees with the species tree, and the gene sits next to mobile-element or insertion-like genes in some genomes, which points to horizontal transfer.
directions.outcomes: Support: clear gene-tree/species-tree conflict, copies in mobile-associated contexts, and base composition unlike the host. Refutation: the gene tree follows the species tree and the neighbourhood is conserved, which means vertical inheritance with lineage-specific loss.
directions.prior_work: PMID 30351021, 35814700 and 37259003 characterise single lanmodulins; none reconstructs how the gene moved among lineages.
directions.question: Lanmodulin occurs only in three alpha-Proteobacterial methylotroph families. Was it inherited from a common ancestor and lost elsewhere, or passed sideways between lineages that share habitats?
directions.readiness_basis: Genome and annotation data are present; tree building and synteny comparison need new computation.
directions.test: Using the Pangenome Collection, build a gene tree for lanmodulin proteins from the bakta-validated genomes and compare it with the species tree. Test whether closely related species differ in carrying lanmodulin. Check the flanking genes of each copy for transposases, integrases and phage genes, and compare the base composition of the gene with its host genome.
directions.title: Was lanmodulin spread by horizontal transfer among alpha-Proteobacterial methylotrophs?
directions.why_it_matters: It would explain the narrow distribution and show whether metal-handling proteins move between lineages in the same habitat, which bears on how lanthanide use evolves.

directions.hypothesis: A large share of xoxF carriers across phyla lack the downstream one-carbon pathways needed to use methanol, so the xoxF-over-mxaF excess reflects broad alcohol oxidation, not methylotrophy.
directions.outcomes: Support: many carriers lack the downstream route and the enzyme prefers longer alcohols. Refutation: nearly all carriers have a complete one-carbon route and the enzyme is most active on methanol.
directions.prior_work: PMID 29404411 and 26858104 show xoxF as the main methanol dehydrogenase in particular methylotrophs and PMID 41636527 reviews wider methylotrophic metabolism; this tests whether the genome-wide excess is methanol-related at all.
directions.question: If xoxF outnumbers mxaF so strongly, do most carriers actually run a full methanol-to-formaldehyde-to-energy route, or does xoxF mainly act on other alcohols or aldehydes in bacteria that are not methylotrophs?
directions.readiness_basis: The genome classification can be done on lakehouse data, but substrate preference requires enzyme assays.
directions.test: In the Pangenome Collection, classify xoxF-carrying genomes by presence of formaldehyde-oxidation and one-carbon assimilation genes, per phylum and with both annotation sources combined. Then, for non-methylotroph carriers in soil lineages such as Acidobacteriota, measure enzyme activity of purified XoxF against methanol, ethanol and other alcohols with and without lanthanides.
directions.title: Is xoxF mostly a methanol enzyme, or does it serve other alcohols in non-methylotrophs?
directions.why_it_matters: It would redefine the xoxF count as a measure of lanthanide-dependent alcohol chemistry, and change how xoxF abundance in soils and wetlands is read as methanol cycling.

directions.hypothesis: Lanthanide-dependent methylotrophs are enriched at lanthanide-rich sites of near-neutral pH but not in acidic, metal-laden drainage, where stress genes dominate.
directions.outcomes: Support: xoxF enrichment at neutral rare-earth-rich sites but not acidic ones, and lanthanum-stimulated enrichments only at neutral pH. Refutation: acidic sites are equally enriched, or neutral rare-earth sites show no excess over matched controls.
directions.prior_work: PMID 33848048 describes the microbiota of a river hit by rare-earth mining drainage, and PMID 38369453 finds lanthanide enzymes in weathered granite and soil; neither compares sites by acidity to see what gates lanthanide-dependent organisms.
directions.question: Acid-mine-drainage genomes from a rare-earth mining site carried little xoxF and no lanmodulin. Does acid and metal stress override lanthanide availability, so that xoxF enrichment appears only at rare-earth-rich sites with milder chemistry?
directions.readiness_basis: The earlier rare-earth set was small and from a single project, so more metagenomes or new enrichments are needed.
directions.test: Search NMDC Multi-omics and NMDC BioSamples for metagenomes from rare-earth-rich soils, weathered rock, mine tailings and acid drainage, plus matched non-rare-earth controls, and compare xoxF and lanmodulin carriage and stress-gene profiles by pH class. Then run methanol enrichments of neutral and acidic rare-earth-rich material with and without added lanthanum, and measure xoxF expression and lanthanide uptake.
directions.title: Do rare-earth-rich sites select lanthanide-dependent methylotrophs only when acidity does not dominate?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that lanthanide supply alone does not recruit lanthanide-dependent organisms and that pH or co-occurring metals gate it. This sets where to look for them in rare-earth mining and recovery settings.

directions.hypothesis: Acid-drainage genomes from rare-earth sites carry lanthanide-binding proteins with calcium-binding-like motifs but no match to known families, and these bind lanthanides more strongly than calcium.
directions.outcomes: Support: candidates enriched at the rare-earth site over the control that bind lanthanides preferentially. Refutation: candidates are equally common in the control or bind calcium as well as lanthanides.
directions.prior_work: PMID 34432449 and 37259003 characterise lanmodulin binding; this searches for binders that annotation-based detection could not find.
directions.question: With no lanmodulin or xoxF in most acid-drainage genomes from the rare-earth site, do those organisms handle lanthanides with proteins that annotation cannot recognise?
directions.readiness_basis: Motif scanning needs new computation and the binding test needs protein expression and spectroscopy.
directions.test: Scan the acid-drainage genomes for proteins with lanmodulin-like or calcium-binding motif patterns and predicted secreted or periplasmic location, excluding those with annotated homologs. Compare their frequency with matched genomes from acid drainage without rare earths. Express the top candidates and test lanthanide and calcium binding by sensitised terbium luminescence.
directions.title: Do rare-earth-rich acid sites use lanthanide-binding proteins unrelated to known ones?
directions.why_it_matters: It would reveal lanthanide-handling systems outside the known protein families and show that gene annotation missed them. It could also give new proteins for rare-earth recovery.

directions.hypothesis: Desulfovibrio vulgaris grows without added serine by making it from glycine and one-carbon units through a non-canonical route, so the predicted gap is a blind spot in the predictor and not an auxotrophy.
directions.outcomes: Growth and labelled serine without added serine, plus a fitness cost for the glycine-to-serine gene, would support a missed route. No growth without serine, and no fitness cost for any candidate gene, would support a true auxotrophy and refute the hypothesis.
directions.prior_work: PMID 29324779 used high-throughput genetics to fill amino acid pathway gaps predicted by automated tools, and PMID 15077118 gives the genome; neither says whether this organism makes serine without a canonical pathway.
directions.question: Is the lack of a complete serine biosynthesis pathway in Desulfovibrio vulgaris Hildenborough a real serine requirement, or does the organism make serine through a route the pathway predictor does not recognise?
directions.readiness_basis: Fitness data and pathway calls are in the lakehouse, but the growth and isotope-tracing experiment has not been done.
directions.test: Grow Desulfovibrio vulgaris Hildenborough in defined serine-free medium with and without glycine and a one-carbon source. Trace labelled glycine into serine. In parallel, read mutant fitness for the serine hydroxymethyltransferase gene and for any partial serine pathway genes in the Fitness Browser, and compare with the other six organisms that have complete calls.
directions.title: Does Desulfovibrio vulgaris make serine by a route that pathway predictors miss?
directions.why_it_matters: The organism was the only one of seven with no complete serine pathway call, and the remaining diversity in amino acid pathways was read as ecological adaptation. If the gap is a missed route, that reading is weaker and pathway predictors have a systematic blind spot in sulfate reducers. If it is real, it is a rare natural serine auxotrophy.

directions.hypothesis: ACIAD3522 is a flavin-dependent enzyme of acetate catabolism, not a respiratory dehydrogenase, and Complex I subunit defects in ADP1 are as strong on acetate and succinate as on quinate.
directions.outcomes: Deletions with a defect only on acetate and a rescue by a downstream intermediate would support a catabolic role. Equal Complex I defects across all four substrates would refute an aromatic-specific bottleneck. Defects confined to quinate would support the flux reading and refute the hypothesis.
directions.prior_work: PMID 18319726 provides the deletion collection and PMID 18840283 the metabolic model; neither tests whether elevated modelled respiratory flux predicts condition-specific essentiality.
directions.question: In Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1, is the gene ACIAD3522 needed for acetate growth because it works in respiratory NADH oxidation, or because it acts in acetate catabolism itself, and is Complex I's aromatic requirement real in ADP1?
directions.readiness_basis: Deletion mutants exist in the published ADP1 collection but growth, redox and rescue data on these substrates are not in the lakehouse.
directions.test: Use the ADP1 single-gene deletion collection to measure growth of the ACIAD3522 deletion and several Complex I subunit deletions on acetate, succinate, quinate and glucose. Add a deletion of a type 2 NADH dehydrogenase if one is found in the genome. Measure NADH to NAD+ balance and test whether acetate-grown deletion strains can be rescued by supplying a downstream intermediate.
directions.title: Is the acetate-specific defect of ACIAD3522 a respiratory role or an acetate catabolism role?
directions.why_it_matters: Higher modelled Complex I flux on aromatics was read as an aromatic-specific bottleneck, while ortholog-transferred defects were strongest on non-aromatic substrates. Settling this decides whether model flux can point to condition-specific essential genes. It would also give a function to a gene the model routes no flux through.

directions.hypothesis: Most unresolved EC-less reactions are catalysed by members of characterised enzyme families acting on a similar substrate, and the matching carbon-source fitness phenotypes point to those family members.
